title: Isogenies and the supersingular graph
one_liner: Maps between elliptic curves, the graph they form on supersingular curves, and why a walk in that graph can be a secret key.
index_meta: Primer · the 2-isogeny graph for p = {{i_p}}, computed and drawn
description: Isogenies between elliptic curves: Velu's formulas worked and checked, j-invariants, the supersingular 2-isogeny graph for p = 431 computed and drawn, walks as keys, and the problems isogeny-based cryptography rests on.
standfirst: An isogeny is a map from one elliptic curve to another that respects addition. On supersingular curves they form a small, tightly connected graph, and every isogeny-based scheme, from SIDH to SQIsign, is built on the difficulty of finding paths in it.

facts.Prime used here: p = {{i_p}} = {{i_p_factor}}, the prime of Costello's tutorial
facts.The graph: {{i_vertices}} supersingular curves over F<sub>{{i_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub>, {{i_edges}} distinct 2-isogeny edges, diameter {{i_diameter}}
facts.Checked at build time: The modular polynomial, the vertex count, Velu's formulas as a homomorphism on {{i_samples}} random pairs of points, and the curve's group order

blocks.p: An isogeny φ: E → E' is a non-constant map between elliptic curves, given by rational functions, that sends the identity to the identity. It is then automatically a group homomorphism: φ(P + Q) = φ(P) + φ(Q). Its kernel is a finite subgroup of E, and for the separable isogenies used in cryptography the degree of φ is the size of that kernel.

Conversely, every finite subgroup G of E is the kernel of an isogeny, unique up to isomorphism of the target, and Vélu's formulas compute it. For a kernel of order 2, generated by a point (x<sub>0</sub>, 0), they are short:

blocks.math:
t = 3x02 + a,   w = x0t,   E': y2 = x3 + (a − 5t)x + (b − 7w)
φ(x, y) = ( x + t/(x − x0),   y·(1 − t/(x − x0)2) )
blocks.label: Vélu's formulas for a 2-isogeny from y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + ax + b.

blocks.p: Worked over F<sub>{{i_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub> = F<sub>{{i_p}}</sub>(i), with i<sup>2</sup> = −1: the curve y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + ({{i_a}})x + ({{i_b}}) has j-invariant {{i_j}} and a 2-torsion point with x<sub>0</sub> = {{i_x0}}. Then t = {{i_t}} and w = {{i_w}}, so the target curve is y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + ({{i_a2}})x + ({{i_b2}}), with j-invariant {{i_j2}}. The point U = {{i_U}} maps to {{i_phiU}}. The build checks that φ(U + V) = φ(U) + φ(V) for {{i_samples}} random pairs of points.

Many equations describe the same curve. Over an algebraically closed field, two curves are isomorphic exactly when they have the same j-invariant, j = 1728·4a<sup>3</sup>/(4a<sup>3</sup> + 27b<sup>2</sup>). So an isogeny graph takes j-invariants as vertices, and joins two of them when an isogeny of the chosen degree connects the curves. The modular polynomial Φ<sub>2</sub>(X, Y) records exactly this for degree 2: Φ<sub>2</sub>(j, j') = 0 if and only if there is a 2-isogeny between curves with those j-invariants. Finding the neighbours of j means finding the roots of the cubic Φ<sub>2</sub>(j, Y).

A supersingular curve over a field of characteristic p is one with no points of order p. There are few of them: every one is defined over F<sub>p<sup>2</sup></sub>, and there are ⌊p/12⌋ + ε of them, with ε between 0 and 2 depending on p mod 12. For p = {{i_p}} that is {{i_formula_floor}} + {{i_formula_eps}} = {{i_vertices}}, and the code that builds this page finds exactly that many by starting at j = 1728 and following roots of Φ<sub>2</sub>.

Every vertex has three 2-isogenies leaving it, counted with multiplicity, so the graph is 3-regular; the vertices j = {{i_loops}} have an isogeny back to themselves. Pizer showed that these graphs are Ramanujan: optimal expanders, in which a random walk reaches an almost uniformly random vertex after O(log p) steps. The layers below show the expansion from j = 1728: the frontier roughly doubles at each step until the graph runs out, and every vertex is within {{i_radius}} steps.

{{i_in_fp}} of the {{i_vertices}} j-invariants lie in the subfield F<sub>{{i_p}}</sub>: {{i_in_fp_list}}. These are the curves defined over F<sub>p</sub>, the setting of CSIDH, where the isogenies form a commutative group action instead of a graph walk.
A walk of e steps is an isogeny of degree 2<sup>e</sup>. Here is one of {{i_walk_len}} steps, the highlighted path in the figure:

blocks.p: Publishing the endpoint and keeping the walk secret is the core of every isogeny key. With {{i_vertices}} vertices anyone can recover a path; with p near 2<sup>256</sup> the graph has about 2<sup>252</sup> vertices, and finding a path between two given curves is the supersingular isogeny path problem. The best classical algorithm, by Wesolowski in 2026, takes time and memory p<sup>1/3+o(1)</sup>. Knowing the endomorphism ring of the endpoints makes paths easy to find, and the two problems are equivalent; this is the Deuring correspondence at work, and it is what SQIsign's signatures prove knowledge of.

The starting curve y<sup>2</sup> = x<sup>3</sup> + x has exactly {{i_count}} = {{i_count_sqrt}}<sup>2</sup> points over F<sub>{{i_p}}<sup>2</sup></sub>, counted point by point at build time. Its group is (Z/{{i_count_sqrt}}Z)<sup>2</sup>, which contains every point of order 2<sup>4</sup> and 3<sup>3</sup>. That is why SIDH used primes of the form 2<sup>a</sup>3<sup>b</sup> − 1: so that walks of 2- and 3-isogenies could be computed from rational torsion points. Publishing the images of those points is what the 2022 attacks exploited.
